## The real Data Table, and why you build it by hand here

In real Excel there's a dedicated command for "what happens to the output if I vary
an input over a series of values": **Data > What-If Analysis > Data Table**.
You use it like this: write the formula ONCE, in a corner, referencing the assumption
cell you want to vary; below or next to that cell put the column (or row) of values to test;
select the whole rectangle — values column included, formula included — and run
the command, giving as **column input cell** exactly the assumption the
formula references. Excel writes, in every cell of the body, an array formula
`{=TABLE(,cell)}`: it substitutes each value of the column into that
input cell, recalculates the formula, and puts the result in the matching row.
Everything stays linked — change the formula at the top and the whole table updates by itself.

*(This trainer doesn't generate the `TABLE()` array formula yet — it's a command that
would need support for multi-cell formulas the game engine doesn't have yet.
The exercise still trains exactly the mechanism that command runs behind the
scenes: substituting a different value row by row and recalculating the same formula.
Here you do it explicitly, once, with the right anchors, and fill it down —
the same numeric result as a real Data Table, written by hand instead of generated.)*

outstanding are **{p2}**. The committee isn't satisfied with a single multiple:
it wants to see the price per share at every EV/EBITDA multiple from **{p3}** to
**{p4}**, in steps of {p5}.

The multiples column is ready: they're the values a real Data Table would have
asked for as the test range. Your job is to write the price-per-share formula
once in the first row, with EBITDA, net debt and shares locked with
the dollar sign — they're the three cells EVERY row looks at, never another — and fill it down
the whole column.

## A grid of what-ifs, not a single number

In real Excel there's **Data > What-If Analysis > Data Table**, the two-variable
version: you write ONE formula in the top-left corner of an empty grid, list
the values of a first parameter along the row above and of a second along the column on the
left, tell Excel which are the two "input cells" (one for the row, one for the
column) — and Excel calculates every crossing on its own, substituting those two values into the formula
and pasting the result into every cell of the grid with an array formula `{=TABLE(...)}`.
Change an assumption upstream and the whole grid recalculates together, without you touching a
single cell of the matrix.

*(This trainer doesn't create the real Data Table in the sheet yet — that's future work
on the game engine, the same note you saw for named ranges. The exercise still trains
exactly the discipline that would make it work: one formula, with three different
anchors, copied across the whole grid — the same idea as M0A-05, but now in two
directions at once instead of a single row.)*

## The case

The target generates a normalised FCF in the last explicit year of **{p0}**.
Before taking it to committee, the desk wants to see how sensitive the implied value is to
two assumptions nobody knows for sure: the **WACC** (the cost of capital used to
discount) and **g** (perpetual growth beyond the explicit horizon). It's exactly the
WACC × g table that closes every real DCF — you'll see it again, fully built, in a later
module.

The implied value for each combination is the Gordon perpetuity: **FCF × (1 + g) /
(WACC − g)**. The rule that holds the formula together: **WACC must always stay above
g**, otherwise the denominator goes to zero or negative and the number stops making
sense — looking at the grid, notice how quickly the value RISES as WACC gets
closer to g: that's why no real DCF trusts a single point.

WACC goes from {p1} to {p2} in steps of 50 basis points,
along the rows. g goes from {p3} to {p4} in steps of 25 basis
points, along the columns. The FCF sits in a single boxed cell: it's the number every
cell of the matrix must look at, never another place on the sheet.

## Solving backwards

Usually a formula starts from the inputs and arrives at a result. Here the problem is the
other way round: you know the result you want — a precise gross margin — and you have to find
the input — the price — that produces it.

In real Excel there's a tool made exactly for this: **Goal Seek**,
under **Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek**. You fill in three
fields — **Set cell** (the formula you want to bring to a certain value), **To value**
(the number you want to see there), **By changing cell** (the only cell Excel may move
to get there) — and Excel tries different prices until the calculated margin comes back
as required.

*(This trainer doesn't have the Goal Seek interface yet: it's a game engine
feature not yet implemented. The concept can still be trained, and here it's
even quicker to do it by hand — the relationship between price and margin is linear, so
two lines of algebra are enough where a solver would have to iterate.)*

## The algebra

Gross margin is defined as: `margin = (price - cost) / price`. You want the price
that brings that margin to a target M, knowing the cost C. Solve for the price:

`M = (P - C) / P`  →  `M·P = P - C`  →  `C = P - M·P = P·(1 - M)`  →  `P = C / (1 - M)`

That's the formula you'll write: not a number found by trial and error, an equation
solved once, valid for any cost and any target margin.

## The case

The target's CFO has set different target margins for its three sales channels, and has
given you the unit production cost of each. You have to rebuild the price list: the
price that, applied to that cost, achieves exactly the required margin.

## The loop that closes itself

A one-period debt schedule, reduced to its bare ingredients: EBITDA, a debt, a
rate. EBITDA {p0} million, fixed capex {p1} million, tax rate
{p2}, interest rate {p3}, opening debt {p4} million.

The chain is:

**interest -> EBT -> net income -> cash available -> repayment -> closing debt ->
average debt -> interest**

Look at the last arrow: it goes back to the start. Interest is calculated on the AVERAGE debt
of the period (average of opening and closing), but closing debt depends on the repayment, which
depends on the cash left AFTER paying interest. To know how much debt remains you need
to know the interest already; to know the interest you need to know how much debt remains.

It's not a design flaw in the sheet: that's how a real debt schedule with
interest on average debt works, in every investment bank. And there is NO order in which
to calculate the cells one at a time that solves this loop: whichever cell you choose to
calculate first, you'd already need the result of another cell that comes after it.
That's exactly why Excel, faced with a cycle A -> B -> A, normally refuses and
flags `#CYCLE!` (or, in the real program, a circular reference error).

The solution is **iterative calculation**: instead of insisting on an order that doesn't exist, you start
from a provisional value (zero, cold) in every cell of the loop and recalculate the whole
chain again and again, each pass a little closer to the point where the numbers stop
changing. In real Excel you turn it on from **File > Options > Formulas > Enable iterative calculation**,
with **Maximum Iterations = 100** and **Maximum Change = 0.001**: exactly the
two numbers this engine uses by default. In this level iterative calculation is already
on: you don't need to look for it in any menu.

What is NOT automatic is the recalculation: here it runs when you ask for it, with **F9** pressed
from a resting cell (not while you're writing a formula — that F9 does something else, seen in
another level). Write the two formulas that close the loop, then press F9: the engine runs
the sweeps and the numbers settle. If the value still looks wrong, check that you
recalculated BEFORE reading it.

The table below already has every cell of the chain written and locked except two: the
**interest** (B9) and the **closing debt** (B15). They're exactly the two cells that close
the loop — the rest is ready, to keep the focus on the real point of the level.

M0F-04-ITERATIVO.23: Closing debt = opening debt minus repayment: `=B6-B14`. Then F9 again to see the converged value.

In real Excel, **Home > Conditional Formatting > New Rule** lets the sheet
decide when to colour a cell: "if the value exceeds X, red background" — and from then
on, every time the number recalculates, the colour updates by itself. That's how you
make a problem visible (a breached covenant, a variance outside threshold) instead of
having to hunt for it row by row.

## Three outfits you read without thinking

A number format doesn't change the number, only how Excel draws it — you've already seen that with currency and percentage. Here are three **custom** formats, the kind that have no dedicated shortcut and are copied from a cell that already has them:

- **Accounting format** `{FORMATO_CONTABILE}` — negatives in **parentheses**, never with a minus sign. It's the standard of every IB/PE model: a negative variance lost in a column of positive numbers is visible at a glance only if it doesn't share the same "-" as a subtraction dash typed by hand.
- **Multiple** `{FORMATO_MULTIPLO}` — a ratio like EV/EBITDA reads as "x", not %.
- **Thousands scale** `{FORMATO_MIGLIAIA}` — the format's trailing comma divides by 1,000 only in the view: the number stored in the cell isn't touched.

None of these three has a dedicated key combination, and this trainer doesn't yet have a "Format Cells" dialog to type them by hand. The solution is the one used in a real model too when the formatting standard is already set elsewhere in the sheet: **you copy the format**. Each block below has a locked "Sample" cell, already dressed in the right format — copy it (`Ctrl+C`), select the cell where you wrote your formula, and paste ONLY the format with `Ctrl+Alt+V` then `T`: the content of the target cell doesn't change, only how Excel draws it.

## Grouping rows: the detail opens only when needed

A long deal model — dozens or hundreds of rows — is never read all laid out.
It's read **in collapsed groups**: only the subtotals, the closed sections, the numbers that
really matter at that moment. The detail opens only when you need to check it.

In real Excel you do this with **row grouping (outline)**: you select the
detail rows, then **Data > Outline > Group** (or the direct shortcut,
**Alt+Shift+Right**), and to the left of the row numbers an outline bar appears with
a **"−"** symbol: clicking it hides the detail and only the subtotal row stays visible,
with a **"+"** in its place to reopen it when needed. To ungroup you use
**Alt+Shift+Left**. It's the same principle as the outline levels
(1, 2, 3...) you see in the top-left corner of the outline bar: a click
on "1" collapses everything, a click on "2" opens only the first level, and so on.

*(This trainer doesn't create a real outline yet — collapsing/expanding rows is a command that would need support for sheet structure the game
engine doesn't have yet; the Alt+Shift+Right/Left shortcuts already exist in the
key map but with no logic behind them. The exercise still trains exactly what STAYS
visible when a group closes: you build the detail block exactly as it would look inside an open group, and the subtotal exactly as it would look with
that group collapsed — it's the number the rest of the model relies on.)*

## The model that checks itself

Every serious model hides a question that should be obvious: "how do I know whether
this sheet is right?" The professional answer isn't "I reread it carefully" — a
sheet with hundreds of cells isn't reread, it's checked. A **sanity check** is a
formula that automatically verifies a property the model MUST satisfy: assets
equal to liabilities plus equity, sources equal to uses in an LBO, the percentages of
an allocation adding up to 100%. If it isn't true, the sheet tells you on its own, straight away,
instead of in a meeting with the client.

Two rules of the trade, not optional:

1. **The check measures the gap, not the total.** `=SUM(range)-100%` is more useful than
   `=SUM(range)`: a total of 99.97% still requires mental arithmetic to see whether it's
   a problem; a gap of -0.03% says it on its own, and a gap close to zero is almost
   always just rounding — well beyond that, it's a real error.
2. **The check is always visible.** It goes next to the data it checks, NEVER hidden at the bottom of the
   sheet or on another tab where nobody looks: a check that isn't visible
   is as good as not written. In real models it often becomes a red/green flag with
   conditional formatting — here you build it as TRUE/FALSE,
   the same logic before the paint.

M0F-09-FUNZIONIDATA.7:
## Dates are numbers, even when they move

You already know: a date in Excel is a number, the count of days since 1 January 1900. The three
functions in this level work on that number, but still return a date-number,
so they're read with the same `dd/mm/yyyy` format — the clothes change, the content doesn't.

- **EOMONTH(date, months)** — the last day of the month, N months later (or earlier, with a negative
  number). It doesn't matter how many days that month has: EOMONTH knows already.
- **EDATE(date, months)** — the very same date, N months later. The day of the month doesn't change,
  only the month (and the year, if needed).
- **YEARFRAC(start, end)** — the fraction of a year between two dates. A 6-month period gives 0.5,
  an 18-month one 1.5: that's how you annualise a figure that covers a non-standard period.

The reference date (B2) is built with `=DATE({anno},{mese},{giorno})`, not typed by
hand: it's the same thing you do when you assemble a date from three separate numbers instead of
typing it in full.

M0F-10-COMBOAUDIT.8:
## The broken model

We close the basic module with the exercise closest to the real job: a piece of a model
**already built by someone else**, which you must check, not write from scratch. None of the
formulas already there returns an Excel error — no `#REF!`, no `#DIV/0!`. They're
all **silent**: plausible numbers that look right until you check them row by
row. They're also the most dangerous kind of error, because nobody flags them.

## The case

A quick three-year projection for the investment committee. Base revenue {p0},
expected growth {p1} a year, expected EBITDA margin {p2}. In year 3
there are {p3} of one-off costs, already inside reported EBITDA: normalising
means adding them back. Then {p4} of depreciation and an overall tax rate of
{p5}.

## Three suspect numbers

The reviewer has already run a general check and flags that **three numbers** in this
statement don't add up — without saying why, only which:

1. **Year 2 revenue**
2. **Year 3 normalised EBITDA**
3. **Year 3 EBIT**

Check them one by one. For each: open the cell (F2), really read what it holds — is it a
calculation or a number typed by hand? — and if needed trace the precedents with **Ctrl+[**.
None of the three will ever be an absurd number: they're all the same order of magnitude as the
right value, which is exactly why it's worth checking them one by one instead of
trusting them at a glance. Write the correct value of each in the column next to it (D): the
original formulas stay locked, the task is to understand what they SHOULD produce, not
to fix them on the sheet.
